subject: Feature Request; Ability to knit an output file agaain ?

messages.author: 2725a0ee59db8261
messages.subject: Feature Request; Ability to knit an output file agaain ?
parts:
Hello,

I've got a particular scenario (use-case) in my head that knitr might
be great for. I want to produce a report of an experiment that
several people are collaborating on. I am doing the data analysis but
others are doing some of the intepretations and conclusions. I want
to have a source file with R code in that I can run through a process
(sweave | knitr) to produce an output file with the results / tables /
graphs. I will then share that with the others who may make changes
to the words, move things around or possibly change the R code
slightly. I then want to periodically take that file and run my
process (sweave | knitr) on it again, which should update the
results / tabls / graphs from R but leave everything else as it was.

I don't think this is currently possible, but could it be done ?

Thanks,

Paul.

messages.author: cc1ef8c8158d6b73
messages.subject: Re: [knitr] Feature Request; Ability to knit an output file agaain ?
parts:
Hi Paul,

I see the great value in this idea, and I have even thought hard about
it in the beginning of the knitr design. In fact this is what an ideal
knitting/weaving engine looks like in my mind, but later I still
surrendered to Sweave and adopted the current model (replace source
code with output).

Hadley's decumar package follows your idea, and the implementation is
roughly like this:

% begin_r_chunk
% opt1: value1
% opt2: value2
% # R code here
% rnorm(10)
% 1 + 1
% end_r_chunk

You write everything in comments, and after you have evaluated the
code, the output is put after the R code, and the source code is still
there in comments. Next time when you run the code again, only the
output is replaced. This model guarantees you always operate on one
single document.

This is why I complained about the WEB/Noweb/Sweave syntax in the end
of this page: http://yihui.name/knitr/demo/minimal/ The traditional
model (<<>>= and @) not only broke the syntax of other document
formats, but also ignored this possibility of putting source code (in
comments) and output together.

Well, since you brought this back to me with a potential application,
I will reconsider this model again. It may not be terribly difficult
to implement, and one difficulty as I can see for the time being is
how to deal with inline R code. Thanks!

BTW, before I proceed, I think you may play with version control tools
for collaboration (like GIT or SVN), but everybody should only edit
the source document. If anyone wants to see the real output, he/she
has to compile it based on the current version of the source document.

Regards,
Yihui

messages.author: 0c39e60ddb38622b
messages.subject: Re: [knitr] Feature Request; Ability to knit an output file agaain ?
parts:
Hi:

The last paragraph of Yihui's note is important. One of the very
useful applications of Git is collaborative writing. One of the
participants controls the master document, and others can add
modifications by creating branches of the master and then placing
their changes in a branch. When one is finished, the branch is pushed
to GitHub and the participant sends a pull request to the owner of the
master branch. That person can then pull the (sets of) changes into
the master document, make additional modifications as necessary and
then push the result back to GitHub. The process is iterated to
convergence. Each new set of changes is placed in a separate branch.
By keeping changes in separate branches, it is possible to maintain a
revision history of who made which changes at which times. This
requires some education about how Git works, but it's something worth
considering.

HTH,
Dennis

messages.author: ef320bb57b221495
messages.subject: Re: Feature Request; Ability to knit an output file agaain ?
parts:
You could use git and block tex files.  Rnw files contains documentation.  Write code in a separate R file.  R code can then be included in the document by defining a new variable

<<setup, echo = FALSE>>
REVIEW <- TRUE
@

Then use:

\SweaveOps{echo =  REVIEW}

Easy code inclusion in the text file.  This works most easily if there is just one switch, i.e. all code or no code + 'hardcoded' echo values. 

Have you seen this page:
   http://yihui.name/knitr/demo/externalization/

messages.author: cc1ef8c8158d6b73
messages.subject: Re: [knitr] Re: Feature Request; Ability to knit an output file agaain ?
parts:
Yes, things should be easier if they follow the version control model
to take advantage of the automatic merging feature.

Yet another idea is to further modularize the process (just like
programming), e.g. use \input{summary.tex} for the person who is going
to write conclusions, and he/she is only in charge of that single
file, so each time you can send the compiled results to him/her and
this person does not need to mess with R code or results.

Regards,
Yihui
